A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same D3M research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including the additional Appendix C in v3.

before.justification: v1 reports original monitoring experiments on UCI Heart Disease, CIFAR-10/10.1, Camelyon17 and the internal medicine dataset, including Table 2, Figures 2–3 and Appendix B.6.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds original ablation and computational analyses in Appendix C, including Tables 8–12 and Figures 7–9.

M1.justification: The feature extractor, VBLL training objective, posterior and categorical sampling, calibration and quantile-based deployment test are unchanged. Fully Bayesian and linear-head alternatives are evaluated as ablations; they do not replace or modify the proposed D3M procedure.

E1.justification: Figure 9 adds a trained-model illustration using noisy Two Moons data. The principal datasets and clinical shift scenarios are retained: GEMINI identifies the previously anonymized IM dataset, with the same patient counts, prediction task and splits.

E2.justification: Appendix C adds linear-head and fully Bayesian model comparisons in Tables 8 and 12. The main benchmark and clinical comparator sets remain unchanged; Domain Classifier was already evaluated and identified as an alias of CTST in v1.

E3.justification: Appendix C introduces substantial additional evaluation designs: controlled head comparisons using accuracy, F1, AUROC and MCC; FLOP accounting at query size 100; temperature and calibration-round sweeps; and training-accuracy checks of maximally disagreeing hypotheses. These are new protocols, while the retained benchmark splits, hyperparameters and query sizes are unchanged.

E4.justification: The new Appendix C tests head replacement, computational cost relative to Detectron, temperature sensitivity, threshold stability, sampling outside the theoretical hypothesis set, and fully Bayesian alternatives. These directly investigate design choices and failure mechanisms beyond v1's supplementary larger-query results, which remain in Appendix B.6.

E5.justification: Table 2 retains means and standard deviations from ten independently seeded runs. New sampling diagnostics specify 1,000 calibration realizations in C.4 and 10,000 runs in C.5; these do not establish increased repetition of the original benchmarks. Section 5 also calls the retained standard deviations confidence intervals without supplying an interval-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 2 and 7 retain their numerical results, and the clinical plots retain their findings. Substantial new results quantify design tradeoffs: Table 9 reports CIFAR compute totals of 1.69 PFLOPs for D3M versus over 3.51 for Detectron, while Table 11 reports selected-hypothesis training accuracies of 0.65 and 0.55 against base-model validation accuracies of 0.76 and 0.70 on UCI and CIFAR respectively. Figures 7–9 add temperature-response and sampling-diversity findings.

T1.justification: Appendix A retains the mathematical definitions, assumptions, idealized algorithms, bounds, failure cases and proofs. Section 2.5 and Appendix C explain and empirically examine the practical approximation without adding or revising a formal guarantee.

C1.justification: Both versions claim efficient, label-free and training-data-free deterioration monitoring, conditional theoretical guarantees, and validation on vision and clinical data. The additional ablations support these existing contributions; the stronger emphasis on GEMINI's clinical relevance does not materially redefine the core claims.

C2.justification: v1 already acknowledged that sampling might leave the ideal hypothesis set. v3 develops this into a substantive interpretation of observed oversampling, arguing that shared calibration bias may preserve discrimination while increasing false negatives. It also adds temperature-gap explanations, fuller clinical-shift interpretation, and explicit discussion of the theory's restriction to ground-truth labeling functions.

D1.justification: v3 identifies the anonymized clinical dataset as GEMINI and adds ablation-specific details, including ImageNet-1K pretraining attribution and the Two Moons generation settings. The principal hyperparameter tables, hardware disclosures and D3M code-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds dataset and software references, including the two GEMINI studies, Krizhevsky, Asuncion and Pedregosa, while removing four healthcare/edge-computing references accompanying the deleted edge-deployment paragraph. The main related-work organization and positioning against disagreement and shift-detection methods remain substantially intact.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose are retained. Local revisions include Section 2.5, the Appendix C organization, expanded clinical discussion and conclusion, replacing few-shot terminology with query sizes, identifying IM as GEMINI, author information changes and conversion to author–year citations.

P2.justification: v3 adds five comparison tables and three figures, including a four-panel temperature analysis and a five-panel decision-boundary illustration. Existing displays are largely retained, with localized formatting changes and a correction of Figure 2(b)'s vertical-axis label from TPR to FPR; that correction does not change the plotted results.

improvement.justification: The new head, cost, sensitivity and sampling studies test important design choices that v1 mainly justified verbally, and make the gap between theory and implementation clearer. However, Section 2.5 still asserts approximate inheritance of guarantees without a new bound, and C.3's claimed increase in FPR conflicts with Figure 7's roughly stable FPR. The added evidence and transparency support a limited net improvement despite these unresolved issues.
